Abstract:

Localization is a fundamental phenomenon in quantum systems arising from the&nbspinterplay of quantum interference and interactions. However, in realistic systems,&nbspdephasing due to the interaction with the environment can significantly affect&nbsplocalization properties. This thesis aims to investigate the effect of dephasing&nbspon localization in Hermitian and non-Hermitian quantum systems. We will first address the question of whether&nbsplocalization can survive dephasing in non-interacting systems and investigate its&nbspimplications for transport in closed and open systems. Subsequently, we will&nbspstudy the effects of dephasing on many-body localization, quantum dynamics, and&nbspentanglement entropy in Hermitian interacting systems and extend similar investigations&nbspto non-Hermitian interacting systems. In particular, we will examine how different&nbspforms of non-Hermiticity influence localization properties and transport behavior under&nbspdephasing. These studies are expected to provide a comprehensive understanding of the&nbsprole of dephasing in localization and establish the similarities and differences between&nbspHermitian and non-Hermitian interacting systems.
